newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Radio Pacific buys 7 Radio Otago stations.
newsitem.headline: Radio Pacific buys 7 Radio Otago stations.

text.p: Radio Pacific said on Thursday its subsidiary, Energy Enterprises, had purchased the operating assets of Radio Otago's seven North Island stations.
In a separate statement, Radio Otago said the sale price was NZ$3.53 million and included the transfer to Radio Otago of Energy Enterprises' four South Island frequencies.

"The acquisition of the Otago assets, which follows the merger of our interests with Energy on April 1, means that in one month Pacific has more than doubled its annual turnover and consolidated itself as the leading provider of radio programmes in the North Island provincial centres," Radio Pacific said.
It said the Radio Pacific Group would have an operating cashflow of nearly NZ$6 million in 1997/98.

"In addition to the Energy and Otago purchase, Radio Pacific has recently registered an interest in acquiring the four FM frequencies that The Radio Network is required to sell following its purchase of the Prospect Group of stations from the British broadcaster GWR," Radio Pacific said.
"Should we be the successful purchaser, shareholders should not expect these frequencies to provide additional cash flows in the immediate future."
It said its board had decided the best option for all shareholders in terms of funding was to borrow, but also to ensure the company returned to a cash position as rapidly as possible.
"To achieve that objective the final dividend due for payment in July, will be five cents per share, bringing the total dividend for 1996/97 to 15 cents per share," Radio Pacific said.
"Directors anticipate that the 1997/98 full year dividends should be at least 15 cents per share."
Radio Otago said the North Island operations sold comprised stations in Tauranga, Rotorua, Taupo, Hawkes Bay and Wanganui.
Radio Otago said it retains the debtors ledgers, valued at approximately $1 million.

John Farry, Chairman of Radio Otago, said in recent times the trend towards multi-station ownership in individual markets had "seen us spread a little too thinly in the North with consequent negative impact on our bottom line".
"This move will immediately strengthen our profitability," Farry said.
He said the move out of the North Island was only the first step in a strategic programme of restructuring and repositioning which would place the company in a much stronger overall position.
